addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

I need to find all background workers, runners, and scheduling infrastructure in this server codebase. Search very thoroughly for:

1. Any background worker classes or functions that get started by the server
2. Scheduling mechanisms (cron, intervals, timers, job queues, task schedulers)
3. Where the server main entry point starts these workers
4. Any scheduling infrastructure that exists in the codebase but might NOT be used

Look for patterns like:
- "worker", "runner", "scheduler", "cron", "interval", "periodic", "background", "job", "task", "queue"
- Timer/setInterval patterns
- Thread/process spawning for background work
- Any scheduler or cron libraries being used

Search breadth: very thorough. Check server startup code, main entry points, worker directories, and any scheduling-related files.

I now have the complete picture. Here is my thorough report.

---

## Background Workers, Runners, and Scheduling Infrastructure

### 1. Server Entry Point and Startup Flow

**Main entry point:** `/bench/home/work/cmd/memos/main.go`
- The `main()` function runs `rootCmd.Execute()` via Cobra.
- The root command creates the server via `server.NewServer()`, then calls `s.Start(ctx)`.
- A goroutine (line 99) listens for SIGINT/SIGTERM and calls `s.Shutdown(ctx)`.

**Server startup:** `/bench/home/work/server/server.go`
- `Server.Start()` (line 101) launches the HTTP server in a goroutine (line 124), then calls `s.startBackgroundRunners(ctx)` (line 129).
- `Server.Shutdown()` (line 134) calls `stopBackgroundRunners()`, `closeLongLivedConnections()`, `shutdownHTTPServer()`, and `waitBackgroundRunners()` in sequence.

---

### 2. Background Runners Started by the Server

#### A. S3 Presign Runner (ACTIVELY USED)
**Files:**
- `/bench/home/work/server/runner/s3presign/runner.go`
- Started in `/bench/home/work/server/server.go` lines 153-173

**How it works:**
- `startBackgroundRunners()` creates an `s3presign.Runner`, calls `RunOnce(ctx)` synchronously for an initial pass, then launches `Run(s3Context)` in a goroutine.
- `Run()` uses `time.NewTicker(12 * time.Hour)` -- it runs every 12 hours to refresh presigned S3 URLs for attachments.
- It iterates through all S3 attachments in batches of 100, and re-presigns URLs that will expire within the next 4 days (URLs have a 5-day expiration).
- Cancellation is handled via context; the cancel function is stored in `s.backgroundRunnerCancels`.
- The `sync.WaitGroup` (`s.backgroundRunnerWG`) tracks the goroutine for graceful shutdown.

#### B. Memo Payload Runner (NOT STARTED AS BACKGROUND WORKER)
**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/runner/memopayload/runner.go`

**Status:** This runner exists but is NOT started by the server at startup. It has a `Runner` struct with a `RunOnce()` method that rebuilds payloads for all memos in batches, but the server never calls `memopayload.NewRunner()` or `RunOnce()` at startup. The only usage of this package is the standalone function `memopayload.RebuildMemoPayload()` called inline during memo creation (line 108) and memo updates (line 447) in `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go`. The `Runner.RunOnce()` batch-processing method appears to be unused production code -- it may have been intended for data migrations or administrative use but is not wired into any startup path.

---

### 3. Async Worker Pools (Started via `init()`)

#### C. Webhook Async Dispatch Workers (ACTIVELY USED)
**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/webhook/webhook.go`

**How it works:**
- An `init()` function (line 42) spawns **4 goroutines** that read from a buffered channel (`asyncPostQueue`, capacity 128).
- Each goroutine calls `Post()` to deliver webhooks synchronously over HTTP.
- `PostAsync()` (line 184) enqueues payloads; if the queue is full, the event is dropped with a warning log.
- These workers start automatically when the `webhook` package is imported, which happens through the import chain: `server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go` imports `internal/webhook`.
- Called from `DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook`, `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook`, `DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook`, and `DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook` in `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go`.

#### D. Email Async Send Workers (ACTIVELY USED)
**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/email/email.go`

**How it works:**
- An `init()` function (line 17) spawns **2 goroutines** that read from a buffered channel (`asyncEmailQueue`, capacity 128).
- Each goroutine calls `Send()` to deliver emails synchronously via SMTP.
- `SendAsync()` (line 55) enqueues email requests; if the queue is full, the email is dropped with a warning log.
- These workers start automatically when the `email` package is imported.
- Used by the `EmailDispatcher` in `/bench/home/work/server/notification/email.go` (line 30), which defaults to `email.SendAsync` as its sender function.

---

### 4. Other Background Goroutines

#### E. Cache Cleanup Goroutines (ACTIVELY USED)
**File:** `/bench/home/work/store/cache/cache.go`

**How it works:**
- `cache.New()` (line 76) launches a `cleanupLoop()` goroutine.
- The cleanup loop uses `time.NewTicker(5 * time.Minute)` (configured via `CleanupInterval`) to periodically evict expired items.
- **3 cache instances** are created in `/bench/home/work/store/store.go` (lines 51-53): `instanceSettingCache`, `userCache`, and `userSettingCache`. This means **3 cleanup goroutines** run continuously.
- Each cache has: DefaultTTL=10min, CleanupInterval=5min, MaxItems=1000.
- `Store.Close()` (line 72) stops all three cache cleanup goroutines.

#### F. SSE Hub + Heartbeat (ACTIVELY USED, per-connection)
**Files:**
- `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/sse_hub.go`
- `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/sse_handler.go`

**How it works:**
- The `SSEHub` is created in `NewAPIV1Service()` and stored on the `Server` struct (line 77 of `server.go`).
- Each SSE client connection gets a `time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)` heartbeat ticker (line 64 of `sse_handler.go`) to keep the connection alive.
- The hub broadcasts events (memo created/updated/deleted, reactions, comments) to all connected clients with per-user visibility filtering.
- On shutdown, `Server.closeLongLivedConnections()` calls `sseHub.Close()` which disconnects all clients.

#### G. PAT Usage Recording (ACTIVELY USED, fire-and-forget)
**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/auth/authenticator.go`

**How it works:**
- `recordPATUsage()` (line 179) spawns a fire-and-forget goroutine to update the "last used" timestamp of a Personal Access Token.
- This is not a persistent worker but an on-demand goroutine spawned per PAT-authenticated request.

---

### 5. Scheduling Infrastructure That EXISTS But Is NOT USED

#### H. Internal Scheduler Package (NOT USED IN PRODUCTION)
**Directory:** `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/`

**Files:**
- `scheduler.go` - Full cron scheduler with `Start()`/`Stop()`, job registration, goroutine-per-job execution
- `job.go` - Job definition struct with Name, Schedule (cron expression), Timezone, Handler, Description, Tags
- `parser.go` - Full cron expression parser supporting 5-field and 6-field formats (with seconds), wildcards, ranges, lists, steps
- `middleware.go` - Composable middleware: `Recovery()`, `Logging()`, `Timeout()`, and `Chain()`
- `doc.go` - Package documentation
- `README.md` - Comprehensive documentation with examples
- `example_test.go`, `integration_test.go`, `scheduler_test.go`, `job_test.go`, `middleware_test.go`, `parser_test.go` - Full test suite

**Status:** This is a fully-implemented, well-tested, zero-external-dependency cron scheduler package. However, it is **never imported outside of its own test files**. The grep for `"github.com/usememos/memos/internal/scheduler"` across the entire codebase returns hits only in `example_test.go` and `integration_test.go`. No production code in `server/`, `cmd/`, or anywhere else imports or uses it. It appears to be infrastructure built for future use or a recent addition not yet integrated.

---

### 6. No External Scheduling Libraries

The `go.mod` file contains no external scheduling/worker/queue libraries (no robfig/cron, gocron, asynq, machinery, river, faktory, etc.). All scheduling is implemented in-house.

---

### Summary Table

| Component | Location | Type | Actively Used? | Started By |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S3 Presign Runner | `server/runner/s3presign/runner.go` | Ticker (12h interval) | Yes | `Server.startBackgroundRunners()` |
| Memo Payload Runner | `server/runner/memopayload/runner.go` | Batch processor (no loop) | `RebuildMemoPayload()` only; `Runner.RunOnce()` unused | N/A (not started) |
| Webhook Workers (x4) | `internal/webhook/webhook.go` | Channel worker pool | Yes | Package `init()` |
| Email Workers (x2) | `internal/email/email.go` | Channel worker pool | Yes | Package `init()` |
| Cache Cleanup (x3) | `store/cache/cache.go` | Ticker (5min interval) | Yes | `cache.New()` in `store.New()` |
| SSE Heartbeat | `server/router/api/v1/sse_handler.go` | Per-connection ticker (30s) | Yes | Per HTTP request |
| PAT Usage Recording | `server/auth/authenticator.go` | Fire-and-forget goroutine | Yes | Per PAT-auth request |
| Cron Scheduler | `internal/scheduler/` | Full cron scheduler | **No** (not imported) | Never started |
